sentence: En Bannons inaugurele rede mag heel agressief en weinig subtiel zijn, hij zit  retorisch goed in elkaar. Ondanks de enorme inhoudelijke afwijking van zowel  Republikeinse als Democratische voorgangers eeuw, haalt hij pakkende  Amerikaanse clichés aan, zoals de, ooit door Franklin Roosevelt geïntroduceerde  ’vergeten man’, die vanaf nu niet meer vergeten zal worden. Als Trump zegt ’Wij  zullen onze manier van leven niet aan anderen opleggen, maar zullen een  stralend voorbeeld zijn’, neemt hij afstand van de Amerikaanse traditionele  rolopvatting als mondiale brenger en beschermer van vrijheid en democratie.  Toch klinken de woorden die hij gebruikt wel traditioneel. Ze doen denken aan  de woorden van een van de eerste Britse kolonisten in Amerika, John Winthrop,  die in 1630 zijn medekolonisten voorhield: ’wij zullen als een stralende stad  op een heuvel zijn; de ogen van de wereld zijn op ons gericht’. Ronald Reagan  was ook dol op die frase. Maar voor hem betekende deze dat Amerika zich  internationaal als gidsland moest opstellen. Trump neemt het beeld wel over,  maar de implicaties voor Amerikaans buitenlandbeleid nadrukkelijk niet. Het slotakkoord is Trumps eigen inmiddels spreekwoordelijke zin  waar iedereen  al de hele speech op had zitten wachten: Make America great again. Het is  interessant, en pijnlijk, om te zien dat ook de oppositie er niet vanaf komt.  Make America sane again, de slogan die Hillary Clinton en velen met haar nu  gebruiken, onderstreept de kracht van Trumps retoriek meer dan dat het een  alternatief biedt.  De taal en de mediaframes die tegenwicht kunnen bieden aan Bannon en zijn  nationalistische krachtpatserij, moeten nog worden bedacht. Her en der hoor je  aanstekelijke uitdrukkingen als resistance (verzet) en civil disobedience  (burgerlijke ongehoorzaamheid), maar het ontwikkelen van een effectief tegengif  staat in de kinderschoenen.  Hier ligt een belangrijke taak voor Amerikaanse schrijvers en voor iedereen die  kritisch tegenover de huidige ontwikkelingen staat. Hopelijk horen we over vier  jaar dan weer iets gezelligers.

hlead: Discussion with Author Jonathan Alter; Interview with Actress Isabella Rossellini A political conversation with Jonathan Alter, author of "The Defining Moment: FDR`s First One Hundred Days and the Triumph of Hope." Director Peter Bogdanovich talks to actress Isabella Rossellini about her new film, "My Dad is 100 Years Old." BOB SCHIEFFER, GUEST HOST: Welcome to the broadcast. I`m Bob Schieffer of CBS News , sitting in tonight for Charlie Rose. And we`re going to begin this evening with a political conversation with Jonathan Alter. His new book is "The Defining Moment: FDR`s First One Hundred Days and the Triumph of Hope." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JONATHAN ALTER, AUTHOR: He saved capitalism and democracy, not once but twice. Everybody knows how he contributed to saving it during World War II, and most of the books about FDR in the last 35 years have been about World War II. So I said, I`m going to kind of leave that alone except in the epilogue, and I was focused on how he saved capitalism and democracy in just a few weeks in 1933, and also redefined the whole bargain -- that`s why they call it the New Deal -- the bargain, that social contract that people had with - with their government.

Director Peter Bogdanovich talks to actress Isabella Rossellini about her new film, "My Dad is 100 Years Old." BOB SCHIEFFER, GUEST HOST: Welcome to the broadcast. I`m Bob Schieffer of CBS News , sitting in tonight for Charlie Rose. And we`re going to begin this evening with a political conversation with Jonathan Alter. His new book is "The Defining Moment: FDR`s First One Hundred Days and the Triumph of Hope." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JONATHAN ALTER, AUTHOR: He saved capitalism and democracy, not once but twice. Everybody knows how he contributed to saving it during World War II, and most of the books about FDR in the last 35 years have been about World War II. So I said, I`m going to kind of leave that alone except in the epilogue, and I was focused on how he saved capitalism and democracy in just a few weeks in 1933, and also redefined the whole bargain -- that`s why they call it the New Deal -- the bargain, that social contract that people had with - with their government.

Director Peter Bogdanovich talks to actress Isabella Rossellini about her new film, "My Dad is 100 Years Old." BOB SCHIEFFER, GUEST HOST: Welcome to the broadcast. I`m Bob Schieffer of CBS News , sitting in tonight for Charlie Rose. And we`re going to begin this evening with a political conversation with Jonathan Alter. His new book is "The Defining Moment: FDR`s First One Hundred Days and the Triumph of Hope." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JONATHAN ALTER, AUTHOR: He saved capitalism and democracy, not once but twice. Everybody knows how he contributed to saving it during World War II, and most of the books about FDR in the last 35 years have been about World War II. So I said, I`m going to kind of leave that alone except in the epilogue, and I was focused on how he saved capitalism and democracy in just a few weeks in 1933, and also redefined the whole bargain -- that`s why they call it the New Deal -- the bargain, that social contract that people had with - with their government.

sentence: JONATHAN ALTER: I think he changed. He never was an intellectual. I mean, Herbert Hoover was much, much more intelligent than he was, but I think he deepened his understanding of Washington when he was assistant secretary of the Navy under Woodrow Wilson. He understood how to get things done in government, the gearing of government, which is really important. Because just passing laws is not enough. You have to make it happen. So he learned that as a bureaucrat.

sentence: BOB SCHIEFFER: What could today`s modern politicians learn from Roosevelt? I think one thing you have just stressed is staying in touch, because my observation, after being in Washington for more than three decades, is that when you come right down to it, the White House is the easiest place -- maybe in the entire country -- to become disconnected from reality. Nobody comes in there unless it`s by the president`s invitation. People have a hard time ever telling the president what they really mean. And you`re cut off, you have the whole federal government at your disposal. I think it`s very easy for any president to almost cut himself off from reality. But you`re saying that Roosevelt found a way to stay connected with reality.

sentence: And I think Roosevelt, even though he did in later years run up the deficit, he understood that you had to ask people to sacrifice. And he was a little bitter at the fact that the wealthy were not appreciative of what he had done for them. He had saved them in 1933, saved their fortunes. He compared it -- excuse me -- to a life guard who saves a drowning man in a silk hat, and then four years later the man comes back and says, "hey, where`s my hat?" And by that time, they had become very critical of him and had forgotten that they would have been in the poorhouse if he hadn`t rescued capitalism.

sentence: And you know, a lot of people wanted him to nationalize the banks. The New Dealers, his liberal base, wanted him to have a government takeover of the banks. The fallback position were postal banks. Can you imagine if the post office ran all our banking? Roosevelt said no, I`m going with a conservative approach, the Hoover approach. We`re going to keep banking in private hands. So he was always cutting left and right at the same time. He was not an ideologue. He was a very, very pragmatic president.

Director Peter Bogdanovich talks to actress Isabella Rossellini about her new film, "My Dad is 100 Years Old." BOB SCHIEFFER, GUEST HOST: Welcome to the broadcast. I`m Bob Schieffer of CBS News , sitting in tonight for Charlie Rose. And we`re going to begin this evening with a political conversation with Jonathan Alter. His new book is "The Defining Moment: FDR`s First One Hundred Days and the Triumph of Hope." (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) JONATHAN ALTER, AUTHOR: He saved capitalism and democracy, not once but twice. Everybody knows how he contributed to saving it during World War II, and most of the books about FDR in the last 35 years have been about World War II. So I said, I`m going to kind of leave that alone except in the epilogue, and I was focused on how he saved capitalism and democracy in just a few weeks in 1933, and also redefined the whole bargain -- that`s why they call it the New Deal -- the bargain, that social contract that people had with - with their government.

headline: Study: 'Job Killer' Claims Usually Go Unsubstantiated
hlead: Study: 'Job Killer' Claims Usually Go Unsubstantiated By Arthur Delaney Huffington Post The phrase "job killer" is rarely substantiated when it appears in news stories, according to a study published Thursday morning. The analysis, conducted by Peter Dreier of Occidental College and Christopher R. Martin of the University of Northern Iowa , examined every occurrence of the phrase or one of its variants, like "kill jobs" or "job-killing," in articles by the Associated Press , The New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the Washington Post going back to 1984. Of the 381 stories that contained the phrase -- usually in a source's quote -- fewer than 10 percent substantiated it. "The news media's chronic lack of fact checking has only encouraged ramped up use of the 'job killer' allegation as a political strategy against the Democrats in recent years," the study says.
